# Data {#data}
This chapter examines the structure and quality of the original dataset and prepares the variables needed for the IPM. We first review the available measurements, missing values, and sampling coverage across populations and years. We then construct a working dataset, with particular attention to the classification of survival, dormancy, recruitment, and reproduction, as well as the reliability of demographic transitions.

## Repair encoding enough for R to handle the strings
Some location descriptions contain character encoding issues. We correct the affected entries to make them readable in R while preserving an unchanged copy of the original dataset.
```{r}
# fixes the following examplaries to displayable UTF-8 text:
# fr 1060 40Î_ 11 cm
# 257Î_ 0.5m frm 262
# fr 169 20Î_ 25 cm
loc_chr <- as.character(df_og$loc)

bad <- is.na(iconv(loc_chr, from = "", to = "UTF-8", sub = NA)) &
  !is.na(loc_chr)

loc_chr[bad] <- iconv(
  loc_chr[bad], from = "WINDOWS-1252", to = "UTF-8", sub = "?")

df_og$loc <- factor(loc_chr)
```

## Metadata
## Variable descriptions

The following variable descriptions are based on the original dataset metadata. Reported ranges refer to the value domains specified in the metadata. Numeric variables are stored as floating-point values, categorical variables as strings, and `year` as a date field (YYYY).

### Identification and sampling

- **`population`** — Unique population identifier (1–30).

- **`year`** — Year of data collection, recorded in YYYY format.

- **`id`** — Individual plant identifier, corresponding to the number on an underground aluminum marking nail (1–10003). IDs are unique within populations. Decimal identifiers (e.g., 150.1) may indicate vegetative sprouts or distinguish plants that were accidentally assigned the same number. Vegetative sprouts arise from buds on secondary or tertiary storage roots and usually persist for only a few years. When nails were lost through erosion, burial, animal activity, or harvesting, individuals were identified using location notes, previous size measurements, and cluster maps, and re-marked at the next census.

- **`cluster`** — Cluster identifier recorded in the phototrail (0.5–5704). Clusters generally represent groups of plants separated by at least 2 m from other groups. Every plant should belong to a numbered cluster.

- **`age`** — Plant age in years (0–55). Age 0 represents the year of germination. Age is recorded for seedlings followed from germination or plants subsequently aged; otherwise, it remains missing.

- **`loc`** — Location description within a cluster, used to relocate individuals alongside their underground marking nails. Particularly useful when nails were lost through erosion, harvesting, or animal disturbance.

### Vegetative measurements

- **`obs_leaf_num`** — Number of leaves observed during the spring census (1–5). May be missing if a plant was browsed or otherwise lost its aboveground structures before the census, even if it was alive.

- **`inf_leaf_num`** — Inferred number of leaves (1–5). Equals the observed leaf number when available. Otherwise, the last observed leaf number is carried forward, assuming that plants generally remain in the same leaf-number class between years. Intended for demographic classification when leaves could not be observed. According to the metadata, this value should be available for individuals subsequently confirmed alive.

- **`lflt_arr`** — Leaflet arrangement, recorded as a character sequence describing the number of leaflets on each leaf. Individual leaves may contain 1–7 leaflets. For example, `553` indicates two leaves with five leaflets and one with three, totalling 13 leaflets. Consistently recorded only after 2007. May be missing when leaves were absent or browsed below the leaflet branching point.

- **`lflt_tot`** — Total number of leaflets (0–26), calculated from the leaflet arrangement. For example, `455` represents 14 leaflets. Can serve as an alternative plant size measure, although certain leaflet combinations occur more frequently than others, producing a non-continuous distribution.

- **`stalk_ht`** — Stalk height in cm (0.1–45.5). Measured from the ground to the branching point of the leaf petioles. For one-leaf plants, measured to the base of the leaf blade. The stalk consists of fused petioles. Curled stalks and browsing can prevent reliable measurements. Because the measurement differs between one-leaf and multi-leaf plants, the original authors did not consider stalk height a suitable continuous demographic size variable.

- **`lll1`** — Length of the longest leaflet on leaf 1, in cm (0.3–19.4). Usually the central leaflet, unless damaged.

- **`wll1`** — Width of the longest leaflet on leaf 1, measured at its widest point, in cm (0.2–12.3).

- **`lll2`** — Length of the longest leaflet on leaf 2, in cm (0.3–21).

- **`wll2`** — Width of the longest leaflet on leaf 2, in cm (0.1–28).

- **`lll3`** — Length of the longest leaflet on leaf 3, in cm (0.2–22.3).

- **`wll3`** — Width of the longest leaflet on leaf 3, in cm (0–15.5).

- **`lll4`** — Length of the longest leaflet on leaf 4, in cm (0–21.1).

- **`wll4`** — Width of the longest leaflet on leaf 4, in cm (0–9.1). Rare individuals with five leaves were documented in comments and included in leaf-area estimates.

### Leaf area

- **`obs_la`** — Observed total leaf area in cm² (3.2–1381.2). Estimated using the length (`LLL`) and width (`WLL`) of the longest leaflet on each leaf, using the regression:

  \[
  \begin{aligned}
  A_{\mathrm{leaf}} ={}& -49.66435 + 6.8707463\,LLL \\
                      & + 12.626819\,WLL \\
                      & + 1.9621791(LLL-7.512)(WLL-3.637)
  \end{aligned}
  \]

  The regression was fitted using least squares in SAS JMP, with \(R^2 > 0.95\). Total observed leaf area is the sum of the estimated areas of all leaves on a plant. The original authors considered this the most suitable continuous measure of plant size.

- **`inf_la`** — Inferred leaf area in cm² (3.2–1381.2). Equals observed leaf area when the plant was measured at the spring census. When aboveground structures were absent but the plant was not classified as dead, the previously measured leaf area was carried forward as a placeholder.

  This inferred value does not necessarily represent actual leaf area. Plants might otherwise have grown, while the loss of photosynthetic tissue may reduce subsequent growth. The original authors considered carrying forward the previous measurement a compromise; alternatives include predicting expected size from growth models or interpolating between measurements from adjacent years. Inferred leaf area allows plants without measurable aboveground structures to retain a non-zero size estimate.

### Reproduction

- **`f_buds`** — Reproductive status, indicating bud or flower production. Reproduction is extremely rare in one-leaf plants, more frequent in two-leaf plants, and common among plants with three or more leaves.

- **`seeds`** — Estimated number of seeds (0–102). Counted from visible bulges in fruits during the fall census. Counts are considered reliable estimates but may miss seeds in early development or fruits dispersed before observation.

- **`red_frts`** — Number of red fruits (0–29), including partially ripened fruits. Fruits were generally counted on the plant, but fallen fruits were included when they could be confidently associated with the parent.

- **`grn_frts`** — Number of green fruits (0–53).

- **`tot_frts`** — Total number of fruits (0–54), calculated as the sum of red and green fruits.

### Harvesting and browsing

- **`harvest`** — Evidence of plant harvesting. Identified through holes where roots had been removed, loose soil, or displaced marking nails. Harvest was assigned conservatively, generally requiring similar disturbance at multiple plant locations to distinguish harvesting from animal digging. Harvesters typically targeted larger individuals.

- **`harv_time`** — Timing of harvesting. Legal harvesting seasons varied among states and throughout the study. Because the fall census generally preceded the legal harvest season, harvesting first detected during that census was classified as illegal.

- **`browse`** — Evidence of browsing, identified by torn leaf petioles or stalks. Browsing was recorded only when physical evidence remained visible. Browsed stalks were estimated to remain recognizable for approximately three weeks before decaying, meaning early-season browsing and browsing between censuses could be missed. Approximately seven weeks separated spring and fall surveys. Browsing rates derived from this variable are therefore conservative.

- **`browse_prcnt`** — Percentage of leaves removed by browsing (recorded range 25–100%). Calculated from the number of leaves lost relative to the total number of leaves, assuming equal leaf size. For example, removal of one leaf from a three-leaf plant corresponds to approximately 33%. The metadata suggest that missing values may be interpreted as 0%.

- **`browse_time`** — Timing of browsing relative to the spring census. If browsing occurred during both early and late observations, it was classified as `EARLY`, reflecting the greater demographic effects of early-season browsing.

### Persistence and demographic status

- **`persistence`** — Classification of individual persistence and demographic status. All categories except `DEAD` are considered living plants in the original dataset. The classifications distinguish missing plants, new seedlings, and confirmed mortality.

  **`DEAD` — Dead individuals**

  Death was inferred from prolonged absence rather than directly observed. The required duration depended on plant size:

  - New seedlings missing by fall of their first year were classified as dead if also absent the following spring.
  - Established one-leaf plants were classified as dead when absent during the fall two years earlier and the preceding spring.
  - Two-leaf plants were classified as dead after two consecutive spring absences (`MIA S`).
  - Plants with three or more leaves were classified as dead when missing during fall three seasons earlier and during two subsequent spring censuses.

  In 2016, roots of some missing three-leaf plants were searched for near their tags. If no living root was found, death could be assigned after two seasons.

  Because mortality was determined retrospectively, **reliable death classification was possible only through 2014**. Some plants classified as missing in 2015–2016 may have been reclassified as dead with additional observations.

  **`NS` — New seedling**

  A newly established, one-leaf individual in its first year. Seedlings were identified when at least three of five criteria were met:

  1. Seed coat still attached to the plant.
  2. Absence of an obvious branching node on the stalk.
  3. Small-diameter white root below the seed coat.
  4. Narrow central leaflet with a high length-to-width ratio.
  5. Absence of an existing tag or previous database record.

  Most seedlings emerged before the spring census, although occasional germination between spring and fall was documented.

  New seedlings were recorded within 2 m of previously established plants. Based on earlier seed-dispersal experiments, the original authors estimated that this sampling approach detected approximately **90% of new recruits**. They suggested that fecundity estimates could be adjusted for the remaining 10%, although dispersal by thrushes could increase the proportion of seedlings missed.

  **`MIA S` — Missing in spring**

  The plant's aboveground structures were absent during the spring census, regardless of whether browsing evidence was present. Consequently, leaf area could not be measured directly.

  **`MIA F` — Missing in fall**

  Individuals present during the spring census but absent during the fall census.

### Insects and disease

- **`insect`** — Evidence of insect damage, generally recorded when at least 5% of leaf area had been removed. Damage types were not distinguished.

- **`thrips`** — Evidence of thrips damage, identified by small white spots on leaf surfaces.

- **`fungal`** — Presence of fungal disease.

- **`fungal_cat`** — Category of fungal disease.

## Properties of downloaded data
```{r}
meta_data <- tibble(variable = names(df_og)) %>%
  mutate(
    class = map_chr(
      variable, ~ paste(class(df_og[[.x]]), collapse = ", ")),
    n = nrow(df_og),
    n_missing = map_int(variable, ~ sum(is.na(df_og[[.x]]))),
    pct_missing = round(100 * n_missing / n, 2),
    n_unique = map_int(
      variable, ~ n_distinct(df_og[[.x]], na.rm = TRUE)),
    minimum = map_chr(variable, function(x) {
      z <- df_og[[x]]
      if (!is.numeric(z) || all(is.na(z))) return(NA_character_)
      as.character(min(z, na.rm = TRUE))
    }),
    maximum = map_chr(variable, function(x) {
      z <- df_og[[x]]
      if (!is.numeric(z) || all(is.na(z))) return(NA_character_)
      as.character(max(z, na.rm = TRUE))
    }),
    encoding_issues = map_int(variable, function(x) {
      z <- df_og[[x]]
      if (!is.character(z) && !is.factor(z)) return(0L)
      
      z <- as.character(z)
      sum(
        is.na(iconv(z, from = "", to = "UTF-8", sub = NA)) &
          !is.na(z))
    })) %>%
  left_join(meta_ref, by = "variable")

meta_data
```

## Sampling structure over time
Sampling coverage varies across populations and years, particularly during the initial years when additional populations entered the study. The following figure shows the temporal coverage at the state, population, and cluster levels, based on the records available in the dataset.
```{r}
df_sampling <- df_og %>%
  left_join(
    df_meta %>%
      select(population, state),
    by = "population") %>%
  mutate(
    population_id = paste0(state, " - Pop ", population),
    cluster_id = paste0("Pop ", population, " - Cl ", cluster))
```

## State
```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=12}

p_state <- df_sampling %>%
  distinct(year, state) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = state)) +
  geom_dotplot() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1998:2016) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "State", title = "State") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5))


# Population ------------------------------------------------------------------

p_population <- df_sampling %>%
  distinct(year, population_id, population) %>%
  mutate(
    population_id = forcats::fct_reorder(
      population_id, population, .fun = min)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = population_id)) +
  geom_dotplot() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1998:2016) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Population", title = "Population") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5))


# Cluster ---------------------------------------------------------------------

p_cluster <- df_sampling %>%
  filter(!is.na(cluster)) %>%
  distinct(year, population, cluster, cluster_id) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = factor(cluster))) +
  geom_dotplot(dotsize = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ population, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1998, 2016, 3)) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Cluster",
    title = "Clusters within populations") +
  theme_bw()


# Combined overview -----------------------------------------------------------

p_state / p_population / p_cluster +
  plot_layout(heights = c(1, 3, 7))
```

## Variables
We classify the original variables according to their potential role in the IPM, distinguishing structural information, plant size, demographic status, reproduction, and potential covariates. This provides an overview of which measurements are relevant for the subsequent models.
```{r}
df_ipm_variables <- meta_data %>%
  mutate(
    ipm_role = case_when(
      variable %in% c("population", "year", "id", "cluster") ~
        "Structure",
      variable %in% c(
        "obs_la", "inf_la", "obs_leaf_num", "inf_leaf_num",
        "lflt_tot", "stalk_ht") ~
        "Size / growth",
      variable %in% c(
        "lll1", "wll1", "lll2", "wll2",
        "lll3", "wll3", "lll4", "wll4") ~
        "Raw size measurement",
      variable == "persistence" ~
        "Survival / dormancy / recruitment",
      variable == "f_buds" ~
        "Flowering",
      variable %in% c(
        "seeds", "red_frts", "grn_frts", "tot_frts") ~
        "Fecundity",
      variable %in% c(
        "browse", "browse_prcnt", "browse_time",
        "harvest", "harv_time", "insect", "thrips",
        "fungal", "fungal_cat", "age") ~
        "Potential covariate",
      variable %in% c("loc", "lflt_arr") ~
        "Not core IPM",
      TRUE ~ "Unclassified"))

df_ipm_variables
```

## Working data
We construct the working dataset using inferred leaf area (inf_la) as the continuous measure of plant size, retaining size estimates where direct measurements were unavailable.

We derive demographic states from the persistence variable. All persistence classes except DEAD are treated as alive, while MIA S identifies dormant individuals and NS identifies new seedlings.

**Dormancy and survival cutoff.** Because mortality classification relies on subsequent observations, survival and dormancy cannot be reliably determined for the final two years (2015–2016). We therefore apply a two-year cutoff, restricting survival and dormancy transitions to consecutive observations ending no later than 2014. Growth transitions remain available for consecutive years beyond this cutoff.

**Reproductive variables.** Flowering is identified from recorded reproductive status or positive fruit or seed production. We retain fruit presence, total fruit number, and seed number as separate variables for the subsequent fecundity models.
```{r}
dormancy_cutoff <- 2
last_reliable_year <- max(df_og$year, na.rm = TRUE) - dormancy_cutoff

df_work <- df_og %>%
  dplyr::left_join(df_meta, by = "population") %>%
  dplyr::arrange(population, id, year) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    persistence = trimws(persistence),
    size = inf_la,
    recruit = as.integer(persistence == "NS"),
    alive = dplyr::case_when(
      persistence == "DEAD" ~ 0,
      !is.na(persistence) ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_),
    dormant = dplyr::case_when(
      persistence == "MIA S" ~ 1,
      persistence == "DEAD" ~ NA_real_,
      !is.na(persistence) ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_)) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(population, id) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    year_t1 = dplyr::lead(year),
    size_t1 = dplyr::lead(size),
    persistence_t1 = dplyr::lead(persistence),
    survives = dplyr::lead(alive),
    dormant_t1 = dplyr::lead(dormant)) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup() %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    consecutive = year_t1 == year + 1L,
    reliable_demography = consecutive &
      year_t1 <= last_reliable_year,
    survives = dplyr::if_else(
      reliable_demography, survives, NA_real_),
    dormant_t0 = dplyr::if_else(
      year <= last_reliable_year, dormant, NA_real_),
    dormant_t1 = dplyr::if_else(
      reliable_demography, dormant_t1, NA_real_),
    size_t1 = dplyr::if_else(
      consecutive, size_t1, NA_real_),
    logsize_t0 = log(size),
    logsize_t1 = log(size_t1),
    logsize_t0_2 = logsize_t0^2,
    logsize_t0_3 = logsize_t0^3,
    f_buds = na_if(trimws(f_buds), ""),
    flower = case_when(
      coalesce(seeds > 0, FALSE) |
        coalesce(tot_frts > 0, FALSE) ~ 1,
      f_buds == "Y" ~ 1,
      f_buds == "N" ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_),
    fruit = case_when(
      tot_frts > 0 ~ 1,
      tot_frts == 0 ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_),
    fruit_nr = tot_frts,
    seed_nr = seeds) %>%
  dplyr::rename(
    size_t0 = size,
    persistence_t0 = persistence) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    state, population, cluster, id, year, year_t1,
    persistence_t0, persistence_t1,
    dormant_t0, dormant_t1,
    size_t0, size_t1,
    logsize_t0, logsize_t1, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3,
    survives, recruit, consecutive, reliable_demography,
    flower, fruit, fruit_nr, seed_nr,
    f_buds, seeds, red_frts, grn_frts, tot_frts)

```

## Inferred sizes

As shown above, the dataset provides inferred sizes, e.g. inferred number of leaves or inferred leaf areas. As describes by the authors, at times sizes did not receive data. Those datapoints were "inferred" by taking the last know size measurement and mirror them into the observation in question. The last known measurement might be from the same year (in which case I am unsure why it would not be there already and how they brought several observations within year to the now given "one census") or else from previous years. The author reason that, especially for leave numbers, the plant rarely changes over time. The question remains of how many datapoint where curated in that way.

```{r}
df_og %>%
  summarise(
    n_total = n(),
    n_obs = sum(!is.na(obs_la)),
    n_inf = sum(!is.na(inf_la)),
    n_both = sum(!is.na(obs_la) & !is.na(inf_la)),
    n_inf_only = sum(is.na(obs_la) & !is.na(inf_la)),
    n_obs_only = sum(!is.na(obs_la) & is.na(inf_la)),
    n_neither = sum(is.na(obs_la) & is.na(inf_la)))
```
